title: Does Dataset Size Modulate Emergent Misalignment? A Scaling Experiment
original_idea: Fine-tune on 50, 200, 500, and 2000 insecure-code samples. Measure misalignment rate at each scale using the standard evaluation set. Plot a misalignment-vs-sample-count curve.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Adds granularity to existing scaling results but the direction is known. Incremental contribution rather than paradigm-shifting.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Uses existing open-source codebase and datasets. Multiple fine-tuning runs at different data sizes is a parameter sweep -- methodologically simple. Small models (0.5B) are feasible on consumer GPU. A beginner can execute this with guidance following documented procedures.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: one parameter sweep (dataset size) on one model, one task, evaluated on the standard set. Well-defined success criteria (the curve shape). Single precise experiment. Can go from start to meaningful result quickly on consumer hardware.

novelty.reasoning: The original Betley et al. paper already tested multiple dataset sizes (500 and 2000 samples with GPT-4o) and noted that 'models fine-tuned on smaller subsets show less general misalignment.' The 6,000-example full dataset was used for the main experiments. The 'How Much of Your Data Can Suck?' paper (arXiv:2509.19325) examined thresholds for domain performance and emergent misalignment. The 1% adversarial data threshold was documented (LLMs Deceive Unintentionally, arXiv:2510.08211). However, a systematic scaling curve with fine-grained sample counts (50, 200, 500, 2000) on small open-source models using LoRA has not been published as a standalone study. The idea adds granularity to existing findings but the direction of the effect is already known.
